The **Hungarian National Gallery** (also known as **Magyar Nemzeti Galéria**, pronounced \[ˈmɒɟɒr ˈnɛmzɛti ˈɡɒleːrijɒ]) was established in 1957 as the national art museum. It is located in Buda Castle in Budapest, Hungary. Its collections cover Hungarian art in all genres, including the works of many nineteenth- and twentieth-century Hungarian artists who worked in Paris and other locations in the West. The primary museum for international art in Budapest is the Museum of Fine Arts.

…

[Hungarian National Gallery - Wikipedia > Exhibitions]

The museum displays a number of works from Hungarian sculptors such as Károly Alexy, Maurice Ascalon, Miklós Borsos, Gyula Donáth, János Fadrusz, Béni Ferenczy, István Ferenczy and Miklós Izsó. It also exhibits paintings and photographs by major Hungarian artists such as Brassai and Ervin Marton, part of the circle who worked in Paris before World War II.\[*citation needed*] The gallery displays the work of artists such as Mihály Munkácsy and László Paál.\[1] The museum also holds paintings by Henrik Weber, Károly Markó the Elder, József Borsos, Miklós Barabás, Bertalan Székely, Károly Lotz, Pál Szinyei Merse, István Csók, Béla Iványi-Grünwald, Tivadar Kosztka Csontváry (*Ruins of Ancient Theatre, Taormina*), József Rippl-Rónai (*Models*), and Károly Ferenczy."],"code":"SUCCESS"}},{"url":"https://en.mng.hu/","title":"Home – Hungarian National Gallery","description":"The aim of the Friends of the Museum is to create a dedicated circle of audience for the Museum of Fine Arts and the Hungarian National Gallery together with their affiliated institutions.","relevance":"medium","markdown":{"markdown":null,"code":"NOT_REQUESTED"},"highlights":{"highlights":["[Dedicated Ones > HNG Annual Ticket]

The Vasarely Museum in Budapest offers a unique experience for visitors interested in optical art and geometric abstraction. Dedicated to the life and work of Victor Vasarely, the Hungarian-French artist widely regarded as the father of Op Art, this specialized art museum in Hungary is located in the picturesque Zichy Palace in the Óbuda district. Since opening in 1987, the museum has stood as a key institution for both Hungarian modern art and global abstract movements.

Situated in the heart of Debrecen, the MODEM Centre for Modern and Contemporary Art stands as a leading art museum in Hungary, renowned for its commitment to showcasing both Hungarian and international contemporary art. Since its establishment in 2006, MODEM has played a pivotal role in enriching the cultural landscape of Eastern Hungary, offering a dynamic platform for artistic expression and dialogue.

…

A significant feature of MODEM is its stewardship of the Antal–Lusztig Collection, one of Hungary's most comprehensive private art collections. **19th and 20th Century Paintings** The 19th and 20th Century Paintings Collection, currently comprising 10,000 items, holds Hungarian artworks dating from 1800 to 1945. Its origins reach back to the mid-19th century and the Founding Society of the National Picture Gallery. Based on continuous purchasing, the expanding collection was initially displayed in the National Museum. Learn about the collection

**Sculptures and Medals** Our collection preserves the most prized works of 19th- and 20th-century Hungarian sculpture along with coins, medals and plaques by Hungarian masters from the 19th to 21st centuries. In addition, it contains wax and plaster copies replacing original artworks, as well as coin works made by contemporary artists. Our holdings comprise some ten thousand items. The most outstanding works are displayed at our permanent exhibition. Learn about the collection

[Hungarian National Gallery - Wikipedia]

The **Hungarian National Gallery** (also known as **Magyar Nemzeti Galéria**, pronounced \[ˈmɒɟɒr ˈnɛmzɛti ˈɡɒleːrijɒ]) was established in 1957 as the national art museum. It is located in Buda Castle in Budapest, Hungary. Its collections cover Hungarian art in all genres, including the works of many nineteenth- and twentieth-century Hungarian artists who worked in Paris and other locations in the West. The primary museum for international art in Budapest is the Museum of Fine Arts.

…

[Hungarian National Gallery - Wikipedia > Exhibitions]

The museum displays a number of works from Hungarian sculptors such as Károly Alexy, Maurice Ascalon, Miklós Borsos, Gyula Donáth, János Fadrusz, Béni Ferenczy, István Ferenczy and Miklós Izsó. It also exhibits paintings and photographs by major Hungarian artists such as Brassai and Ervin Marton, part of the circle who worked in Paris before World War II.\[*citation needed*] The gallery displays the work of artists such as Mihály Munkácsy and László Paál.\[1] The museum also holds paintings by Henrik Weber, Károly Markó the Elder, József Borsos, Miklós Barabás, Bertalan Székely, Károly Lotz, Pál Szinyei Merse, István Csók, Béla Iványi-Grünwald, Tivadar Kosztka Csontváry (*Ruins of Ancient Theatre, Taormina*), József Rippl-Rónai (*Models*), and Károly Ferenczy.

The Vasarely Museum in Budapest offers a unique experience for visitors interested in optical art and geometric abstraction. Dedicated to the life and work of Victor Vasarely, the Hungarian-French artist widely regarded as the father of Op Art, this specialized art museum in Hungary is located in the picturesque Zichy Palace in the Óbuda district. Since opening in 1987, the museum has stood as a key institution for both Hungarian modern art and global abstract movements.

Situated in the heart of Debrecen, the MODEM Centre for Modern and Contemporary Art stands as a leading art museum in Hungary, renowned for its commitment to showcasing both Hungarian and international contemporary art. Since its establishment in 2006, MODEM has played a pivotal role in enriching the cultural landscape of Eastern Hungary, offering a dynamic platform for artistic expression and dialogue.

…

A significant feature of MODEM is its stewardship of the Antal–Lusztig Collection, one of Hungary's most comprehensive private art collections. This collection, which includes works by prominent Hungarian artists, is regularly showcased through rotating exhibitions, providing visitors with insights into the evolution of Hungarian modern and contemporary art.

**19th and 20th Century Paintings** The 19th and 20th Century Paintings Collection, currently comprising 10,000 items, holds Hungarian artworks dating from 1800 to 1945. Its origins reach back to the mid-19th century and the Founding Society of the National Picture Gallery. Based on continuous purchasing, the expanding collection was initially displayed in the National Museum. Learn about the collection

**Sculptures and Medals** Our collection preserves the most prized works of 19th- and 20th-century Hungarian sculpture along with coins, medals and plaques by Hungarian masters from the 19th to 21st centuries. In addition, it contains wax and plaster copies replacing original artworks, as well as coin works made by contemporary artists. Our holdings comprise some ten thousand items. The most outstanding works are displayed at our permanent exhibition. Learn about the collection

…

**Library** The Hungarian National Gallery, established in 1957, uses the library that once belonged to the Metropolitan Picture Gallery, as its museum library. The holdings were later expanded with legacies of books left behind by some outstanding art historians (Dénes Radocsay, Gyula Szentiványi, István Genthon, and Gábor Pogány Ö.). The museum library’s volumes have also been augmented in recent years through purchases, domestic and international exchanges as well as donations. Learn about the collection
